title: React Capstone — The Guild Portal
description: Build a complete, deployed React application from scratch. You will architect a multi-page Guild Portal — a quest-browsing app with routing, data fetching, TypeScript, global state, and a live public URL. This is your proof of mastery.

subChunks.title: Project Architecture: Laying the Foundation
subChunks.hookHtml: Every great structure starts with a blueprint. Before you write a single component, you decide how the pieces fit together — folder structure, routing skeleton, shared types. Get this right and the rest flows naturally. Get it wrong and you'll be refactoring forever.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Architecting a React App

The folder structure we'll use

src/
  components/     # Reusable UI pieces
  pages/          # Route-level components (one per URL)
  hooks/          # Custom hooks
  store/          # Zustand stores
  types/          # TypeScript interfaces
  api/            # Fetch helpers
  App.tsx         # Routes live here
  main.tsx        # ReactDOM.createRoot

Routing skeleton first

Define all your routes before you fill in the pages. This forces you to think about navigation flows upfront.

// App.tsx
import { BrowserRouter, Routes, Route } from "react-router-dom";
import { Layout } from "./components/Layout";
import { HomePage } from "./pages/HomePage";
import { QuestsPage } from "./pages/QuestsPage";
import { QuestDetailPage } from "./pages/QuestDetailPage";
import { ProfilePage } from "./pages/ProfilePage";

export default function App() {
  return (
    <BrowserRouter>
      <Routes>
        <Route path="/" element={<Layout />}>
          <Route index element={<HomePage />} />
          <Route path="quests" element={<QuestsPage />} />
          <Route path="quests/:id" element={<QuestDetailPage />} />
          <Route path="profile" element={<ProfilePage />} />
        </Route>
      </Routes>
    </BrowserRouter>
  );
}

Shared TypeScript types

Define your data shapes once, import everywhere. This eliminates an entire category of bugs.

// src/types/index.ts
export interface Quest {
  id: number;
  title: string;
  difficulty: "FOUNDATION" | "PRACTITIONER" | "EXPERT";
  xpReward: number;
  completed: boolean;
  tags: string[];
  description: string;
}

export interface User {
  id: number;
  username: string;
  totalXp: number;
  rank: string;
  completedQuestIds: number[];
}

The Layout component — persistent shell

Use React Router's Outlet to render child routes inside a persistent navbar/shell. The nav never re-mounts; only the page content swaps.

// src/components/Layout.tsx
import { Outlet, NavLink } from "react-router-dom";

export function Layout() {
  return (
    <div className="app-shell">
      <nav className="navbar">
        <span className="brand">⚗️ Guild Portal</span>
        <NavLink to="/">Home</NavLink>
        <NavLink to="/quests">Quests</NavLink>
        <NavLink to="/profile">Profile</NavLink>
      </nav>
      <main className="page-content">
        <Outlet />
      </main>
    </div>
  );
}

NavLink vs Link

NavLink automatically adds an active class when its to matches the current URL — perfect for highlighting the current nav item without manual state.

subChunks.title: The Quest Browser: Data, Filtering, and Lists
subChunks.hookHtml: The beating heart of the Guild Portal is the quest browser. Learners need to see all available quests, filter by difficulty, and find what to tackle next. This page exercises every pattern from the Practitioner tier in one cohesive feature.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Building the Quest Browser

Simulating an API with local data

In a real app you'd fetch from a server. For the capstone we'll use a local mock so you focus on the React patterns, not network setup.

// src/api/quests.ts
import { Quest } from "../types";

const MOCK_QUESTS: Quest[] = [
  { id: 1, title: "The Component Model", difficulty: "FOUNDATION", xpReward: 75,
    completed: true, tags: ["jsx", "components"], description: "Learn JSX and build your first component." },
  { id: 2, title: "Props: Feeding Components Data", difficulty: "FOUNDATION", xpReward: 75,
    completed: true, tags: ["props", "typescript"], description: "Pass data into components via props." },
  { id: 3, title: "State and useState", difficulty: "FOUNDATION", xpReward: 100,
    completed: false, tags: ["state", "hooks"], description: "Add interactivity with the useState hook." },
  { id: 4, title: "useEffect: Side Effects", difficulty: "PRACTITIONER", xpReward: 125,
    completed: false, tags: ["hooks", "effects"], description: "Synchronise with the outside world." },
  { id: 5, title: "Context API", difficulty: "EXPERT", xpReward: 175,
    completed: false, tags: ["context", "state"], description: "Share state without prop drilling." },
  { id: 6, title: "TypeScript with React", difficulty: "EXPERT", xpReward: 200,
    completed: false, tags: ["typescript"], description: "Add full type safety to your components." },
];

// Simulate async fetch
export async function fetchQuests(): Promise<Quest[]> {
  return new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve(MOCK_QUESTS), 300));
}

Three-state loading pattern (typed)

type LoadState = "loading" | "error" | "success";

function QuestsPage() {
  const [quests, setQuests] = useState<Quest[]>([]);
  const [status, setStatus] = useState<LoadState>("loading");
  const [filter, setFilter] = useState<"ALL" | Quest["difficulty"]>("ALL");

  useEffect(() => {
    let cancelled = false;
    fetchQuests()
      .then(data => { if (!cancelled) { setQuests(data); setStatus("success"); } })
      .catch(() => { if (!cancelled) setStatus("error"); });
    return () => { cancelled = true; };
  }, []);
  // ...
}

Derived state via useMemo

const visibleQuests = useMemo(
  () => filter === "ALL" ? quests : quests.filter(q => q.difficulty === filter),
  [quests, filter]
);

The QuestCard component

interface QuestCardProps {
  quest: Quest;
  onSelect: (id: number) => void;
}

function QuestCard({ quest, onSelect }: QuestCardProps) {
  return (
    <div
      className={`quest-card ${quest.completed ? "completed" : ""}`}
      data-testid="quest-card"
    >
      <div className="quest-header">
        <h3>{quest.title}</h3>
        <span className={`badge badge-${quest.difficulty.toLowerCase()}`}>
          {quest.difficulty}
        </span>
      </div>
      <p>{quest.description}</p>
      <div className="quest-footer">
        <span className="xp">+{quest.xpReward} XP</span>
        {quest.completed
          ? <span className="done">✓ Complete</span>
          : <button onClick={() => onSelect(quest.id)}>Start Quest</button>
        }
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the three-state loading pattern (loading / error / success) to someone who just learned useState yesterday — why three states instead of just a boolean?

options: useMemo is required whenever you call array methods in React
useMemo caches the filtered result and only recomputes when quests or filter changes, avoiding unnecessary work on every render
Filtering in render causes an infinite re-render loop
useMemo makes the filter synchronous, whereas inline filtering is asynchronous
questions.explanation: useMemo memoises expensive computations. Filtering a large array on every render (e.g. triggered by an unrelated state change) wastes CPU. useMemo only recomputes when its dependencies change.
questions.prompt: Why use useMemo for the filtered quest list rather than filtering directly in the render?
questions.answer: useMemo caches the filtered result and only recomputes when quests or filter changes, avoiding unnecessary work on every render

options: It prevents duplicate API calls when React strict mode double-invokes effects
It prevents setting state on an unmounted component if the response arrives after navigation away
It prevents the browser from caching the fetch response
It prevents TypeScript from inferring the wrong return type
questions.explanation: If a user navigates away before the fetch resolves, the component unmounts. Without a cancellation flag, the .then() still runs and calls setState on the unmounted component — a React warning and potential memory leak.
questions.prompt: What does the cancellation flag pattern (let cancelled = false) prevent in a useEffect data fetch?
questions.answer: It prevents setting state on an unmounted component if the response arrives after navigation away

options: TypeScript automatically widens the union to include 'ARCHIVED'
The app crashes immediately when the data loads
TypeScript won't error at compile time, but runtime data won't match the declared type — a reminder that TypeScript only validates compile-time structure, not runtime API responses
The browser silently coerces 'ARCHIVED' to undefined
questions.explanation: TypeScript types are erased at runtime. If the API returns a value outside the declared union, TypeScript won't catch it. Use runtime validation (Zod, type guards) for data that crosses an API boundary.
questions.prompt: A QuestCard receives a quest prop of type Quest. Inside the card, you render quest.difficulty. TypeScript shows no error. Later the API adds a new difficulty level 'ARCHIVED' not in the union type. What happens?
questions.answer: TypeScript won't error at compile time, but runtime data won't match the declared type — a reminder that TypeScript only validates compile-time structure, not runtime API responses

options: useEffect(() => { setVisible(...) }, [quests, filter])
useMemo(() => filter === 'ALL' ? quests : quests.filter(...), [quests, filter])
useState(quests.filter(...))
useCallback(() => quests.filter(...), [quests, filter])
questions.explanation: useMemo computes a derived value and caches it. useEffect with setState would cause an extra render cycle. useState initialises once and doesn't react to prop changes. useCallback is for memoising functions, not values.
questions.prompt: You want the quest list to re-filter whenever either quests or filter changes, but not on every render. Which hook and dependency array is correct?
questions.answer: useMemo(() => filter === 'ALL' ? quests : quests.filter(...), [quests, filter])

subChunks.title: Quest Detail Page: URL Params and Navigation
subChunks.hookHtml: A list is only half the picture. When a user selects a quest, they need a full detail view — a separate URL they can bookmark, share, and return to. React Router's useParams and useNavigate make this seamless.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Dynamic Routes and the Detail Page

Reading URL params

// Route defined as: <Route path="quests/:id" element={<QuestDetailPage />} />

import { useParams, useNavigate } from "react-router-dom";

function QuestDetailPage() {
  const { id } = useParams<{ id: string }>();
  const navigate = useNavigate();
  const [quest, setQuest] = useState<Quest | null>(null);
  const [status, setStatus] = useState<"loading" | "error" | "success">("loading");

  useEffect(() => {
    let cancelled = false;
    fetchQuestById(Number(id))
      .then(data => { if (!cancelled) { setQuest(data); setStatus("success"); } })
      .catch(() => { if (!cancelled) setStatus("error"); });
    return () => { cancelled = true; };
  }, [id]); // re-fetch when the id param changes

  if (status === "loading") return <div data-testid="loading">Loading…</div>;
  if (status === "error" || !quest) return <div data-testid="not-found">Quest not found.</div>;

  return (
    <div data-testid="quest-detail">
      <button onClick={() => navigate(-1)}>← Back</button>
      <h1>{quest.title}</h1>
      <span className="badge">{quest.difficulty}</span>
      <p>{quest.description}</p>
      <p>Reward: +{quest.xpReward} XP</p>
      {!quest.completed && (
        <button
          data-testid="accept-btn"
          onClick={() => handleAccept(quest.id)}
        >
          Accept Quest
        </button>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

Programmatic navigation

// Go back in history
navigate(-1);

// Navigate to a specific route
navigate("/quests");

// Navigate and replace (no back button history entry)
navigate("/quests", { replace: true });

// Navigate after an action completes
async function handleAccept(questId: number) {
  await markQuestAccepted(questId);
  navigate("/quests"); // return to list
}

id in useEffect dependencies

Notice [id] in the dependency array. If the user navigates from /quests/3 to /quests/7 the component stays mounted (same route, different param) and the effect re-runs with the new id — fetching fresh data automatically.

Linking from the quest list

import { Link } from "react-router-dom";

// In QuestCard:
<Link to={"/quests/" + quest.id}>View Details</Link>

storyBeats.speaker: Vex
storyBeats.text: The URL is a contract. '/quests/3' should always show quest 3 — whether the user arrives by clicking a card or pasting the link into a new tab. useParams lets you honour that contract.
You focus the URL bar and type the address directly. The detail page loads instantly, every field populated from the id alone. The contract holds.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why id must be in the useEffect dependency array for the detail page, as if explaining to someone who thinks 'it worked without it so why add it?'

options: Nothing — the component is already mounted, so useEffect doesn't re-run
The component unmounts and remounts, triggering the effect from scratch
The effect re-runs because id is in the dependency array and its value changed from '3' to '7'
The effect re-runs only if useNavigate is called inside the component
questions.explanation: React Router keeps the same component mounted for same-pattern routes (/quests/:id). The id param changes, which changes the dependency, which triggers the effect to re-run and fetch the new quest.
questions.prompt: A user navigates from /quests/3 to /quests/7. The QuestDetailPage component is already mounted. What happens to the useEffect that fetches by id?
questions.answer: The effect re-runs because id is in the dependency array and its value changed from '3' to '7'

options: Change Quest.id to string to match useParams
Cast it with Number(id) or parseInt(id) before using it in fetch calls that expect a number
Nothing — JavaScript automatically coerces string '3' to number 3 in all arithmetic
Use parseInt only if the string might contain decimals
questions.explanation: URL params are always strings. If your data model uses number ids, convert explicitly with Number(id) or parseInt(id, 10). Relying on implicit coercion is fragile and breaks TypeScript's type checking.
questions.prompt: useParams returns id as a string even though your Quest type uses number. What should you do?
questions.answer: Cast it with Number(id) or parseInt(id) before using it in fetch calls that expect a number

options: When you want to skip the loading state on the destination page
When you want the navigation to not create a history entry, so the back button skips past it — e.g. after a successful form submission or login
When navigating to an external URL
When navigating within the same page (hash links)
questions.explanation: replace: true replaces the current history entry instead of pushing a new one. This is useful after actions like login or form submission — you don't want users hitting the back button to re-submit the form.
questions.prompt: When should you use navigate('/quests', { replace: true }) instead of navigate('/quests')?
questions.answer: When you want the navigation to not create a history entry, so the back button skips past it — e.g. after a successful form submission or login

options: Link renders faster because it uses a web worker
Link prevents the full-page reload that href causes, enabling client-side navigation and preserving React state
href attributes are not supported in JSX
Link components automatically prefetch the destination page's data
questions.explanation: <a href> causes a full browser navigation — React state is wiped, the bundle is re-parsed. <Link> intercepts the click, updates the URL via the History API, and lets React Router swap components without a reload.
questions.prompt: Why use <Link to='/quests/3'> instead of <a href='/quests/3'>?
questions.answer: Link prevents the full-page reload that href causes, enabling client-side navigation and preserving React state

subChunks.title: The Profile Page: Zustand Store and Persistence
subChunks.hookHtml: A guild portal without progress tracking is just a list. The Profile page needs to know which quests the user has accepted, their total XP, and their current rank — state that persists across page reloads. This is Zustand's home turf.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Global State with Zustand

Defining the store

// src/store/userStore.ts
import { create } from "zustand";
import { persist } from "zustand/middleware";
import { Quest } from "../types";

interface UserState {
  username: string;
  totalXp: number;
  acceptedQuestIds: number[];
  acceptQuest: (quest: Quest) => void;
  reset: () => void;
}

export const useUserStore = create<UserState>()(
  persist(
    (set) => ({
      username: "Apprentice",
      totalXp: 0,
      acceptedQuestIds: [],

      acceptQuest: (quest) =>
        set((state) => {
          if (state.acceptedQuestIds.includes(quest.id)) return state; // idempotent
          return {
            totalXp: state.totalXp + quest.xpReward,
            acceptedQuestIds: [...state.acceptedQuestIds, quest.id],
          };
        }),

      reset: () => set({ username: "Apprentice", totalXp: 0, acceptedQuestIds: [] }),
    }),
    { name: "guild-portal-user" } // localStorage key
  )
);

Using the store in components

// Scoped subscription — component only re-renders when totalXp changes
const totalXp = useUserStore((s) => s.totalXp);
const acceptQuest = useUserStore((s) => s.acceptQuest);

// In QuestDetailPage accept button:
<button onClick={() => acceptQuest(quest)}>Accept Quest</button>

Computing rank from XP

// src/utils/rank.ts
export function getRank(xp: number): string {
  if (xp >= 8000) return "Archmage";
  if (xp >= 4000) return "Mage";
  if (xp >= 2000) return "Adept";
  if (xp >= 800)  return "Apprentice";
  return "Novice";
}

// Usage in ProfilePage:
const totalXp = useUserStore((s) => s.totalXp);
const rank = getRank(totalXp);

The Profile page layout

function ProfilePage() {
  const { username, totalXp, acceptedQuestIds, reset } = useUserStore();
  const rank = getRank(totalXp);

  return (
    <div data-testid="profile">
      <h1>{username}</h1>
      <p data-testid="rank">Rank: {rank}</p>
      <p data-testid="total-xp">Total XP: {totalXp}</p>
      <p data-testid="quest-count">Quests accepted: {acceptedQuestIds.length}</p>
      <button onClick={reset}>Reset Progress</button>
    </div>
  );
}

storyBeats.speaker: Vex
storyBeats.text: Local state dies when the component unmounts. Context dies when the page reloads. Zustand with persist middleware? That outlives the session — it writes to localStorage and reads back on startup. Your XP survives a browser close.
You accept three quests, note the XP counter climb, then refresh the browser. The numbers hold. The scroll remembers.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why Zustand's persist middleware is preferable to storing user progress in a useState inside the ProfilePage component, as if talking to someone who says 'but useState already works fine for me'.

options: Zustand's set function automatically deduplicates calls with the same arguments
In real apps, accept buttons may be clicked multiple times, event handlers may fire twice, or optimistic updates may re-trigger — checking before updating prevents corrupted state
Zustand's persist middleware deduplicates localStorage writes
React Strict Mode calls event handlers twice, so all handlers must be idempotent
questions.explanation: Defensive state updates assume that the same action may fire more than once. Checking `acceptedQuestIds.includes(quest.id)` before updating makes the store reliable regardless of how many times the action is dispatched.
questions.prompt: Why should acceptQuest be idempotent (no double-counting if called twice with the same quest)?
questions.answer: In real apps, accept buttons may be clicked multiple times, event handlers may fire twice, or optimistic updates may re-trigger — checking before updating prevents corrupted state

options: const store = useUserStore(); — read the whole store
const { totalXp } = useUserStore(); — destructure at the call site
const totalXp = useUserStore((s) => s.totalXp); — pass a selector function
const totalXp = useUserStore.getState().totalXp; — read outside React
questions.explanation: Passing a selector function subscribes only to that slice. When other parts of the store change, this component doesn't re-render. Reading the whole store or destructuring from it subscribes to every change.
questions.prompt: Which selector pattern minimises unnecessary re-renders when reading from a Zustand store?
questions.answer: const totalXp = useUserStore((s) => s.totalXp); — pass a selector function

options: It is synchronous and blocks the main thread, so it should be avoided in production
Data survives page reloads and browser restarts without a server, but is browser-specific, has a ~5 MB limit, and is inaccessible to other browsers or devices
localStorage is encrypted by the browser, so persist is secure for sensitive data
persist requires a server round-trip on every store update
questions.explanation: localStorage persistence is great for non-sensitive, device-local data (preferences, draft state). It doesn't sync across devices, has storage limits, and isn't appropriate for sensitive data. For multi-device sync, you'd combine Zustand with a backend API.
questions.prompt: The persist middleware writes to localStorage. What are the tradeoffs of this approach?
questions.answer: Data survives page reloads and browser restarts without a server, but is browser-specific, has a ~5 MB limit, and is inaccessible to other browsers or devices

options: Inside the component — it needs access to the component's state
Outside the component — it's a pure utility with no React dependencies; keeping it outside avoids recreating it on every render
Inside a useCallback — pure functions always need memoisation
Inside a useMemo — it must rerun whenever XP changes
questions.explanation: Pure functions that don't depend on React state or props belong outside components. Defining them inside means a new function identity on every render (harmless but wasteful). The component simply calls getRank(totalXp) inline.
questions.prompt: getRank is a pure function that takes XP and returns a string. Should it be defined inside or outside the React component?
questions.answer: Outside the component — it's a pure utility with no React dependencies; keeping it outside avoids recreating it on every render

subChunks.title: Polish and Accessibility: The Final Layer
subChunks.hookHtml: A working app and a good app are separated by the details: keyboard navigation, screen reader labels, loading states that don't flash, and transitions that feel alive. This is what separates a portfolio piece from a throwaway exercise.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Accessibility and Polish

Semantic HTML first

// ❌ div soup
<div class="nav">
  <div class="nav-item" onClick={...}>Home</div>
</div>

// ✅ semantic — keyboard focusable, screen-reader announced correctly
<nav aria-label="Main navigation">
  <NavLink to="/">Home</NavLink>
</nav>

Icon-only buttons need labels

// ❌ screen reader announces "button" with no context
<button onClick={onClose}>✕</button>

// ✅ aria-label provides the accessible name
<button onClick={onClose} aria-label="Close dialog">✕</button>

Loading states — avoid layout shift

// ❌ nothing visible while loading → jarring pop-in
if (loading) return null;

// ✅ skeleton or spinner with correct ARIA role
if (loading) return (
  <div role="status" aria-live="polite" aria-label="Loading quests">
    <div className="skeleton" />
    <div className="skeleton" />
    <div className="skeleton" />
  </div>
);

Keyboard navigation for filter buttons

// Use role="group" + aria-label on the filter container
<div role="group" aria-label="Filter by difficulty">
  {DIFFICULTIES.map(d => (
    <button
      key={d}
      onClick={() => setFilter(d)}
      aria-pressed={filter === d}  // toggles true/false for screen readers
    >
      {d}
    </button>
  ))}
</div>

Focus management after navigation

// After navigating to the detail page, move focus to the heading
const headingRef = useRef<HTMLHeadingElement>(null);

useEffect(() => {
  headingRef.current?.focus();
}, [quest?.id]); // runs when quest loads

<h1 ref={headingRef} tabIndex={-1}>{quest.title}</h1>
// tabIndex={-1} makes it programmatically focusable without adding it to the tab order

CSS transitions for list re-renders

.quest-card {
  transition: opacity 200ms ease, transform 200ms ease;
}
/* With a key prop, React remounts on filter change →
   add an entry animation class on mount */

prefers-reduced-motion

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .quest-card { transition: none; }
}

storyBeats.speaker: Vex
storyBeats.text: A sighted user with a mouse never notices accessibility work. But a keyboard user, a screen-reader user, a user on a slow connection — they notice every gap. Polish is not decoration. It's respect for your users.
You tab through the entire app without touching the mouse. Every button is reachable. Every state is announced. The portal is complete — not just functional, but considerate.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
🏗️ Guided: Accessible Filter Buttons

Rewrite the quest filter buttons to be fully accessible.

Requirements:

  • Wrap filters in a div with role="group" and aria-label="Filter by difficulty"
  • Each button has aria-pressed="true" when active, aria-pressed="false" otherwise
  • Active button has class active
  • All buttons are keyboard focusable and activatable with Enter/Space (default button behaviour)
  • The filter container has data-testid="filter-group"
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🧩 Solo: Add Skip Navigation

Screen reader users often want to skip repetitive navigation and jump straight to main content.

  • Add a "Skip to main content" link as the very first focusable element in the page — href="#main-content"
  • Style it visually hidden by default (position: absolute; left: -9999px) but visible when focused (:focus { left: 0; })
  • Give the main content area id="main-content" and tabIndex={-1}
  • Add data-testid="skip-link" to the skip link
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why aria-pressed is used on toggle buttons instead of aria-selected or aria-checked, as if a developer just asked 'aren't they all the same thing?'

options: Add title='Close' — tooltips make the button accessible
Add aria-label='Close dialog' — this provides the accessible name to screen readers
Wrap it in a span with text — then hide the span with CSS
No fix needed — screen readers can infer intent from the icon's Unicode name
questions.explanation: aria-label directly provides the accessible name for screen readers without altering the visual design. title only shows on hover and is not consistently announced by screen readers. Hiding text with CSS is a valid alternative but more complex.
questions.prompt: A button renders only an X icon with no visible text. What is the correct accessibility fix?
questions.answer: Add aria-label='Close dialog' — this provides the accessible name to screen readers

options: The element is removed from the DOM entirely
The element is skipped in the natural tab order but can be focused programmatically via .focus()
The element becomes the first focusable element on the page
The element receives focus after all tabIndex={0} elements
questions.explanation: tabIndex={-1} removes an element from the sequential tab order (users can't tab to it) but allows programmatic focus via element.focus(). This is the standard pattern for focus management — e.g. moving focus to a heading or dialog when it opens.
questions.prompt: What does tabIndex={-1} on an element mean?
questions.answer: The element is skipped in the natural tab order but can be focused programmatically via .focus()

options: Animated transitions are deprecated in modern browsers
Some users experience dizziness, nausea, or seizures from motion. Disabling or reducing transitions for users who have enabled this OS-level accessibility setting is a WCAG requirement.
prefers-reduced-motion is only relevant for video content, not CSS transitions
CSS transitions block the main thread and cause jank on low-end devices
questions.explanation: Users with vestibular disorders, epilepsy, or motion sensitivity can set prefers-reduced-motion in their OS settings. Respecting it by disabling or reducing animations is a WCAG 2.1 AA success criterion (2.3.3).
questions.prompt: Why should you respect prefers-reduced-motion in your CSS transitions?
questions.answer: Some users experience dizziness, nausea, or seizures from motion. Disabling or reducing transitions for users who have enabled this OS-level accessibility setting is a WCAG requirement.

options: null is better — fewer DOM nodes means faster rendering
Skeleton is better — it preserves the layout shape so content appears in place rather than jumping into view, reducing cumulative layout shift (CLS) and perceived wait time
Both are equivalent — the user experience is identical
null is better because it avoids the risk of skeleton styles conflicting with content styles
questions.explanation: Returning null causes a content pop-in — the page jumps as content appears. A skeleton (or spinner in a stable container) maintains layout, reduces CLS, and gives users a sense of progress. CLS is a Core Web Vital that affects both UX and SEO.
questions.prompt: Which renders a better loading experience: returning null while data loads, or rendering a skeleton?
questions.answer: Skeleton is better — it preserves the layout shape so content appears in place rather than jumping into view, reducing cumulative layout shift (CLS) and perceived wait time

subChunks.title: The Grand Commission: Deploy the Guild Portal
subChunks.hookHtml: Everything you have built lives only on your machine. A craftsperson's work is only real when others can see it. The Grand Commission is your final act: ship the Guild Portal to a live URL, share it, and claim your Expert badge.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Deploying a Vite + React App

Option A — Vercel (recommended, ~3 minutes)

  1. Push your project to a GitHub repository
  2. Go to vercel.com → "New Project" → import from GitHub
  3. Framework preset: Vite — Vercel detects it automatically
  4. Click Deploy. Done. You get a URL like https://guild-portal-abc.vercel.app
  5. Every push to main auto-redeploys

Option B — Netlify (~3 minutes)

  1. Push to GitHub
  2. Go to netlify.com → "Add new site" → import from GitHub
  3. Build command: npm run build
  4. Publish directory: dist
  5. Deploy. URL like https://guild-portal-abc.netlify.app

Option C — CodeSandbox (no git, ~2 minutes)

  1. Go to codesandbox.io
  2. Create a new sandbox → "Vite + React" template
  3. Paste your component files into the editor
  4. The sandbox URL is live immediately: https://abc123.csb.app
  5. Export → "Fork to GitHub" to make it permanent

Pre-deploy checklist

# Run locally first
npm run build      # Vite compiles to dist/
npm run preview    # Serves dist/ — test this before deploying

# Common issues before deployment:
# 1. Environment variables — any VITE_* vars needed?
# 2. React Router with BrowserRouter — add a _redirects file (Netlify)
#    or configure rewrites (Vercel) so direct URL access works
# 3. Console errors — fix all errors before deploying

React Router on deployed static hosts

BrowserRouter uses real URLs like /quests/3. Static hosts serve files by path — they'll 404 on a direct visit to /quests/3 because there's no file there. Fix:

# Netlify — create public/_redirects:
/*    /index.html   200

# Vercel — create vercel.json at project root:
{
  "rewrites": [{ "source": "/(.*)", "destination": "/index.html" }]
}

What your submission must include

  • ✅ A live URL (Vercel / Netlify / CodeSandbox)
  • ✅ Quest browser page renders and filters work
  • ✅ Quest detail page loads via /quests/:id
  • ✅ Profile page shows XP and rank
  • ✅ Accepting a quest on the detail page increments profile XP
  • ✅ No console errors in production
"The URL is not the destination. It is the proof that the journey happened."
— Grand Archmage Solomon

storyBeats.text: The Grand Archmage Solomon stands at the window of the Academy's highest tower, looking out over the city.

storyBeats.speaker: Solomon
storyBeats.text: From the first component to the final deployment — you have walked the full path. Not every apprentice completes the journey. Many learn. Fewer build. Fewer still ship.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex
storyBeats.text: The concepts will fade if you don't use them. But a URL with your name on it? That you can point to in an interview. That's evidence.

storyBeats.speaker: Solomon
storyBeats.text: Deploy the portal. Submit the URL. The Expert badge awaits — but more than the badge, you earn the right to say: I built something real.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:

Before deploying to a host, run the production build locally and fix any issues.

Steps:

  1. Run npm run build in your project root — fix any TypeScript or build errors
  2. Run npm run preview — open the preview URL and verify all three pages work

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why a React app with BrowserRouter returns a 404 when you directly visit a deep URL on a static host — and why the _redirects fix works — as if explaining to someone who just deployed their first React app and is confused.

options: The page loads correctly — Netlify serves index.html for all routes by default
The page returns a 404 — Netlify looks for a file at /quests/3, finds none, and serves the default 404 page
The page returns a 500 — Vite builds generate broken paths without special config
The page loads but React Router state is reset
questions.explanation: Static file hosts serve files literally. /quests/3 maps to a file at that path, which doesn't exist. The _redirects rule tells Netlify to serve index.html for every path, letting React Router handle routing client-side.
questions.prompt: You deploy a Vite + React app to Netlify without a _redirects file. A user visits https://your-app.netlify.app/quests/3 directly. What happens?
questions.answer: The page returns a 404 — Netlify looks for a file at /quests/3, finds none, and serves the default 404 page

options: No risk — TypeScript errors are compile-time warnings and don't affect runtime behaviour
The undefined value may cause a runtime crash when the component tries to access a property on it, resulting in a white screen error for users
Vercel will refuse to deploy an app with TypeScript errors
The prop will be silently set to null at runtime, preventing a crash
questions.explanation: TypeScript errors are warnings about places where your code's assumptions don't hold. Ignoring them means the edge case is still there — when the undefined value is accessed at runtime (e.g. quest.title on null), you get an uncaught error and likely a broken UI.
questions.prompt: You run npm run build and see a TypeScript error about a prop being potentially undefined. You ignore it and deploy anyway. What is the risk?
questions.answer: The undefined value may cause a runtime crash when the component tries to access a property on it, resulting in a white screen error for users

options: Zustand stores are cleared on refresh — you need to re-fetch from the server
The persist middleware was configured but the storage key changed between builds, invalidating the stored data
The Zustand persist middleware was not included, so state is only in memory and lost on page unload
Vercel clears localStorage between deployments as a security measure
questions.explanation: Without persist middleware, Zustand state lives only in memory. A page refresh is a fresh JavaScript environment — the store re-initialises to defaults. Adding persist with a stable key fixes this by reading from localStorage on startup.
questions.prompt: After deploying, you find a bug: accepting a quest updates XP in the current session but the XP is gone after a browser refresh. What is the most likely cause?
questions.answer: The Zustand persist middleware was not included, so state is only in memory and lost on page unload

options: Accessibility is required by law in most countries, so it must be done first

Accessibility built in from the start costs far less than retrofitting it — semantic HTML and ARIA labels are written once at component creation; fixing a built app requires auditing and rewriting every component
Accessibility improves SEO, so it should be prioritised for business reasons
Modern browsers handle accessibility automatically if you use React
questions.explanation: Retrofitting accessibility is significantly more expensive than building it in from the start. Writing a semantic button instead of a div-with-onClick takes zero extra time. Auditing and rewriting a complete app later does not. The 'later' that never comes is one of the most common quality debts in frontend development.
questions.prompt: A friend says 'I'll add accessibility later once the features are done.' What is the most important counterargument?
questions.answer: Accessibility built in from the start costs far less than retrofitting it — semantic HTML and ARIA labels are written once at component creation; fixing a built app requires auditing and rewriting every component
